nameStory: The Blinded Sphinx gets its name from the distinctive eyespots on its hindwings that appear "blinded" or incomplete compared to other sphinx moths. Unlike many moths with bold, complete eyespots that look like staring eyes, this species has eyespots that are partially obscured or fade out, giving them a clouded, unseeing appearance.
description: The Blinded Sphinx is a medium to large moth with a robust, streamlined body typical of the sphinx moth family. These powerful fliers have forewings that are mottled in shades of brown, gray, and tan, creating excellent camouflage against tree bark. Their hindwings feature the characteristic "blinded" eyespots that give them their name. With wingspans reaching 3-4 inches, they're substantial moths that you're more likely to encounter at dusk than during the day.

idTips.label: Blinded Eyespots
idTips.description: Look for the pale, incomplete eyespots on the pinkish hindwings that appear faded or partially erased, unlike the bold, complete eyespots of many other moths

idTips.label: Forewings
idTips.description: Mottled brown and gray forewings with wavy lines and patches that feel smooth to the touch and provide bark-like camouflage

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Thick, streamlined body that tapers to a point at the rear, built like a tiny fighter jet for fast, hovering flight

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Hovers at flowers like a hummingbird with rapid wingbeats that create a soft humming sound you can hear from several feet away

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings roof-like over the body and presses tight against tree bark where it becomes nearly invisible

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where wild cherry, birch, and willow trees grow - the host plants for their caterpillars. Adults visit gardens, forest edges, and anywhere tubular flowers like honeysuckle, petunias, and bee balm provide nectar. They prefer areas with both woodland cover for daytime roosting and open spaces with flowers for nighttime feeding.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, becoming active at dusk around flowering trees and shrubs. Look for them hovering at lilac and other early blooming flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season when adults are most commonly seen at flowers after sunset. Caterpillars are feeding on host trees during this time but are rarely encountered.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may emerge in early fall, though less common than spring adults. Late-season flowers like cardinal flower may attract them.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil beneath host trees. No adult activity during this season.

funFact: Sphinx moths are sometimes called "hummingbird moths" because they hover at flowers and feed with a long proboscis, but the Blinded Sphinx can actually fly faster than a hummingbird - reaching speeds of up to 37 mph, making them among the fastest flying insects in New England!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative, the Small-eyed Sphinx, but the Small-eyed has complete, bold blue eyespots rather than the faded, incomplete eyespots of the Blinded Sphinx. Remember: "Blinded" means the eyespots look cloudy and incomplete, while "Small-eyed" means the eyespots are complete but just smaller than other sphinx moths.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "sphinx" moths, they have no connection to the ancient Egyptian sphinx - the name comes from the caterpillars' habit of rearing up in a sphinx-like pose when threatened. The scientific name "excaecata" literally means "blinded" in Latin, directly referencing those distinctive incomplete eyespots.
compareHints: The Blinded Sphinx differs from its close relative, the Small-eyed Sphinx, primarily in the eyespot pattern - the Small-eyed has complete, vivid blue eyespots while the Blinded has partial, faded eyespots. The Small-eyed is also generally smaller and has more contrasting colors on its forewings. Both species have similar flight patterns and habitat preferences, but the eyespot difference is unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Blinded Sphinx, the Small-eyed Sphinx has much smaller eyespots on the hindwings and tends to be slightly smaller overall.
